title: Build, Buy, or Defer: Where SaaS Engineering Actually Compounds

Build the capabilities that learn with the business Defer architecture whose business case has not arrived Buy the instrument, keep the operating judgment The framework on one page Engineering attention is the real budget SaaS Software Architecture Software Development Product Management Startup Build, Buy, or Defer: Where SaaS Engineering Actually Compounds Oleksandr Kolesnykov 11 min read · Oct 2, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Engineering attention is finite: build the compounding core, buy bounded capabilities, and defer unproven commitments. An early-stage SaaS company can justify building almost anything. A custom marketing site promises control. A homegrown help center looks small. A reusable integration layer looks responsible. Another monitoring product appears to close an operational gap. Each proposal can make sense on its own. Together, they consume the people who were supposed to be building the business. Custom code is not just an asset. It is an open-ended claim on engineering attention. I have spent 11 years shipping software products, including five years in C-level roles. Across advertising platforms, automation systems, and multi-tenant SaaS products, I have seen the same expensive decisions recur. They rarely come from weak engineers. Building makes progress visible; waiting for evidence does not. The useful question is therefore not build versus buy. It is build, buy, or defer : Build where product knowledge and customer advantage accumulate inside the company. Buy where a focused vendor’s continued investment will outpace what the company should sustain internally. Defer while the need is unproven and waiting remains inexpensive. Applied early, this distinction can save months of work and years of maintenance. The unit of account is ownership Most comparisons put a vendor invoice on one side and an implementation estimate on the other. That is incomplete. The vendor’s number is a quote. The implementation estimate is a forecast made before anyone has found the integration dependencies, missing requirements, migrations, incidents, and support work. The internal alternative is not the ideal system in an architecture document. It is what the current team can ship this quarter, then realistically operate, secure, support, and improve. I use five questions before assigning permanent ownership to the company: What capability does the business need, and what would we actually build now? Compare the vendor with the credible first version, not a perfected future platform. Where will knowledge accumulate? If every customer interaction makes an internal capability more valuable, ownership may create an advantage. Who needs to change it? A founder-operated marketing surface has a different ownership model from a transaction pipeline operated by engineering. How contained and reversible is the decision? Examine failure boundaries, data access, integration depth, portability, and the cost of leaving. What evidence makes today the right time? If waiting is safe and implementation later remains bounded, deferral has value. The decision flow is simple: If domain learning compounds inside the capability, build is the leading candidate. If it does not, and a mature vendor has an acceptable boundary and exit path, buy . If the need is still hypothetical and waiting is cheap, defer . Security, revenue, and reliability obligations override deferral. These are not permanent labels on categories of software. They apply to capabilities, and the right call can change as evidence, operating ownership, and reversal cost change. One complete decision: who should own the marketing site? The marketing site is where this framework changed one of my own defaults. Capability and evidence. PixelFlow , the multi-tenant MarTech SaaS I currently build, needed a credible front door that explained the product, converted visitors, and supported search. I initially assumed engineering should own it. Four full-time engineer-weeks went into a custom Next.js site. It shipped as part of a larger release that also replaced a post-signup stub with a usable site-setup flow. Across matched windows of about 50 days, the release roughly doubled the signup rate. That evidence did not prove that Next.js caused the lift or that engineering should permanently own the website: the story, design, and product experience had changed together. It proved that the front door needed serious work. The ownership cost appeared afterward: the product was evolving, the ideal customer was coming into focus, and the positioning had to change with both. That iteration was part of learning the market, not exceptional rework; the custom site turned each lesson into another engineering task. Credible alternatives. The custom release had clarified the story and shown that regular iteration was necessary, so deferral no longer fit. The remaining options were: keep the Next.js site and retain the design-to-engineering handoff; add Strapi so selected content blocks were editable while layout and responsive changes still required engineering; move the site into a builder where the founder could own copy, layout, and publishing. Strapi would have narrowed the handoff, not removed it. Permanent engineering ownership did not fit either: copy, layout, and publishing were not teaching us anything about conversion tracking that belonged in the product. Operating owner, boundary, and exit. The founder needed direct control. Site edits could still hurt conversion, accessibility, SEO, or marketing analytics, but would not touch core product behavior: billing rules, customer events tracking, tenant permissions, or dashboard workflows.
